steps.title: A gem is not just any stone
steps.text: A gem is a material, most often a mineral, with enough qualities to be worn as jewellery or collected. Not all minerals are gems. And not all gems come from the ground: there are several kinds. Let us see how they are classified.

steps.title: The family of gems
steps.text: There are two big families: • natural gems, formed without people; • non-natural gems, made or assembled by people. Each one is divided again. Follow the tree.

steps.title: Natural gems
steps.text: They formed in nature, even if people later cut or treated them. • Crystalline: the atoms are arranged in a regular pattern. These are the minerals: diamond, ruby, emerald, quartz... • Non-crystalline: no regular order. Either amorphous (opal, obsidian), or organic materials produced by living beings (pearl, amber, coral, jet).

steps.title: Non-natural gems
Five qualities make a gem
steps.text: Natural or not, a stone becomes a gem when it brings together five qualities: beauty, rarity, durability, value and acceptability. Let us go through them.

steps.title: Beauty
steps.text: It is the first quality, the one you see: colour, transparency, luster and, for some stones, fire or light effects (chatoyancy, asterism, opalescence). A beautiful stone catches the eye before any measurement.

steps.title: Rarity
steps.text:
The rarer a stone is, the more it is sought after. Quartz is found everywhere; fine ruby or emerald, very little.

Rarity also plays inside a species: a large, very pure stone of a perfect colour is much rarer than a small ordinary stone.

steps.title: Durability
steps.text: A piece of jewellery is worn every day: the stone must hold up. Three things count: • hardness (resisting scratches), • toughness (resisting blows and chips), • stability (resisting light, heat and chemicals). An opal or a pearl is beautiful but fragile. Each of these three has its own lesson, right after this one on the board.

steps.title: Value
steps.text: Value is the result of the other qualities, but it also depends on size, weight in carats, treatment, origin and the market: supply and demand. Two stones of the same species can be worth a hundred times more or less than each other.

steps.title: Acceptability
steps.text: Finally, the market must accept the stone: customers must want it, fashion or tradition must adopt it, and above all they must be able to trust it. An undisclosed treatment or a synthetic stone sold as natural destroys that trust. This is why gemmologists are needed.

steps.title: Acceptability: the law
Your role
steps.text: These qualities are not guessed: they are measured. The instruments of the laboratory are used to recognize the species, to spot treatments and imitations, and to check quality. Let us start with the first look at a stone: the loupe.
